newsitem.title: GREECE: New Greek cabinet mixes old-guard, reformers.
newsitem.headline: New Greek cabinet mixes old-guard, reformers.

text.p: Greek Prime Minister Costas Simitis mixed old-guard socialists and a new generation of party reformers on Tuesday in his "new era" cabinet at the start of a four-year term.
"During the formation of this cabinet, we sought to combine tested experience with the need for renewal," said a government spokesman before reading out the list.

Simitis, 60, succeeded late socialist party founder and three-time premier Andreas Papandreou in January. A methodical technocrat, Simitis has vowed to reform the party and to change the erratic course of the EU's only Balkan state.
His election win over the opposition conservatives on Sunday gave him a free hand to lay Papandreou's ghost to rest and stamp his own seal of authority on the party and government.

Despite initial hints of radical change, Simitis stayed with tried and trusted ministers. Controversial but competent Foreign Minister Theodoros Pangalos, who occasionally offends EU allies with his blunt comments, stayed at his post.
A German and British-trained economist, Simitis has made his priority meeting strict economic targets set out by the European Union.
He kept the backbone of his economic team intact, renaming Cambridge-educated National Economy Minister Yannos Papandoniou, who drove down inflation to single digits for the first time in 20 years.
The two men have developed a close working relationship over the past eight months and Simitis effectively made Papandoniou his economic "czar", adding the finance ministry to his brief.

"There was always a belief that there should be one minister heading the finance and national economy ministries to ensure better coordination," said John Marcopoulos, Managing Director at Sigma Securities.
"The market's reaction should be positive. It didn't look forward to unpleasant surprises. I expect we will see faster action now on many pending agendas," he added.
Simitis renamed Vasso Papandreou, for years a fellow party dissident, as development minister despite her confrontations with foreign investors, especially over private casinos.
The only major change was the removal of defence minister Gerassimos Arsenis, an old-guard socialist who has criticised Simitis's handling of a crisis with Turkey in January.
In his place Simitis named Akis Tsohatzopoulos, a Papandreou crony, but one who eventually threw his support behind Simitis.
Arsenis angered Simitis with his back-room dealings to gain support for a $10 billion arms build-up. Tsohatzopoulos will cut that purchase to the bone to ensure EU economic targets are met.
The only surprise was a paltry payout to George Papandreou, son of the socialist party founder, who helped turned the tide in Simitis's favour in a bruising leadership battle in June.
Papandreou was named deputy foreign minister, where he will take orders from the blustering Pangalos who is renowned for his fits of temper.
Political commentators said Papandreou, just 44 but wearing the most powerful political name in Greece, made his displeasure known to Simitis about his second-rank appointment.
Simitis, who emerged from the socialist party shadows only recently, has vowed to push lagging Greece into line with its EU partners.

But the only appointment which smacked of real reform was sending Alexandros Papadopoulos, the respected finance minister since 1993, to the interior ministry where he will try to reform a vast and hopelessly ineffective public sector administration.
